verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Nalagarh electrical-equipment and pump/motor units with diversified order books and power back-up, and avoid power-intensive, single-customer units until local demand and power supply stabilise.
title: Nalagarh Electrical Equipment, Pumps & Motors: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**These units buy steel, copper, laminations and bought-out components, wind them and machine them into motors, pumps and switchgear, and sell mostly to institutional and tender buyers.** Cash turns on the order book and on how fast the buyer pays; value sits in the winding and testing shop, not in the building. **Capex is moderate but lumpy** — a new winding line or test bench is a step cost, so utilisation decides margin. Pricing power is thin against organised peers; the lever is cost and order mix, not price.

## What has changed now
**The local economy is contracting while the national motor/pump cycle is expanding.** Himachal GST collections are -22.8% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], and state electricity demand is -6.8% Apr-to-date against India +9.5% [D]. Nationally, IIP for NIC 27 output is +30.9% YoY and +28.5% Apr-to-date [D]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's order book is national or local; if it is local-tender dependent, ask for the last six months of dispatch and receivable ageing.** Local industry has publicly flagged an electricity crisis and sought the CM's help [2], and the Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh cluster is reporting a crime spike and police manpower crunch [1] — both are operating risks, not credit events, but they hit uptime and insurance.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue units feeding national infrastructure and replacement demand** — specialty motors, off-highway and railway applications, where a peer reports complex applications as the valuable segment [4]. **Pursue pump makers with a government or export order book**: one listed peer grew Q1 FY27 revenue 37.9% YoY to ₹859 crore [6][7], and H1 FY27 revenue rose 24.5% YoY to ₹16,047 Mn [5]. **Avoid single-customer job-work units and units with no captive power or DG back-up**; the local power signal [D][2] makes them fragile.

## How to grow safely
**Structure term debt to the asset, not to the order**, and keep working capital as a separate, reviewed limit. **Take every month: dispatch register, receivable ageing, power outage log, and GST returns** — the state GST number [D] is the cleanest early read. **Covenant on DSCR and on receivable days; if receivable days stretch beyond the sanctioned cycle, ask for the buyer-wise ledger and stop enhancement.** Rating reports show this sector is working-capital intensive with heavy capex and equity support [8][9]; a peer with no long-term debt and ₹347 crore of fixed deposits [10] shows what a strong balance sheet looks like — most Nalagarh units will not look like that, so size limits to their own cash cycle.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch power cost per unit and outage hours** — if the borrower cannot show DG run-hours, treat the margin as unproven. **Watch GST turnover against bank credits**; a widening gap means sales are slipping out of the account. **Watch receivable days and buyer concentration**; one buyer above half of sales is a red flag. **Watch for delayed statutory dues and salary delays** — in a cluster with a crime and manpower problem [1], staff attrition shows up in dispatch first. **If any two of these trigger in the same quarter, freeze fresh limits and re-price.**
watch: gap above 10% for two months -> ask for buyer-wise sales ledger and hold enhancement
stretch beyond sanctioned cycle -> stop limit increase, seek buyer confirmation
repeated outages without DG -> re-price or reduce exposure
fall for two months -> review order book and covenant test
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
